insights.headline: She converts every major grief or injustice into an administrative task performed alone before witnesses are told.
insights.explanation: The child who walks two hours to repay a debt in secret (E1), the woman who files a transfer without mentioning it (E2), and the widow who arranges hakajimai — temple, stonemason, permits — before phoning her brother-in-law (E5) all show the same shape: private execution, then announcement. This is not simply thoroughness; in each case the concealment itself is chosen, not incidental, since she had opportunity to include others and declined.

evidence.quote: I told no one. For about a month.
I arranged the whole of it before I told anybody.

insights.would_predict: Health and Wellness: if she receives a serious personal diagnosis, she will research and decide on a course of treatment alone and present it to family as settled, rather than deliberating with them.

insights.headline: She treats being needed as more valuable than being credited, and repeatedly chooses the former over the latter when both are on offer.
insights.explanation: She volunteers for the 'difficult' school where 'you were not handed things, you were simply needed' (E2), calls the vice-principalship — invisible, no face — the truest description of herself (E4), and takes chairmanship offers from the neighborhood association only to hand the visible title to Ueda-san while doing the actual work herself (E5). In all three she has a path to visible authority (principal's exam, committee chair) and exchanges it for functional indispensability instead.

evidence.quote: you were not, ah, you were not handed things, you were simply needed
Ueda-san is chair. He is a good man and he cannot operate a spreadsheet and he telephones me on Sunday evenings.

insights.would_predict: Work and Career: in any future volunteer or advisory role, she will decline the named leadership position while becoming the person the actual title-holder depends on within weeks.

insights.headline: She describes herself as someone who does not object, while her life is a record of engineered, undeclared exits from the arrangements she claims to accept.
insights.explanation: She states plainly "I did not object" to twelve years of pouring tea (E2, L12-13) and frames her marriage as something she simply fit inside (E3). Yet the same person spent months reading obscure transfer regulations to escape the tea-pouring hierarchy (E2), used Sundays alone as a secretly cherished non-marital space (E3, L28), and later closed a family grave and dissolved a forty-year household's rituals unilaterally (E5) — none of which is 'not objecting,' all of which are self-authored departures dressed as continuity.

evidence.quote: I have read things since where women say they objected and perhaps they did, but I did not.
I have never told anyone that Sunday was my favorite day and that it was my favorite day because he was not there.

insights.would_predict: Relationships: in a current friendship or community conflict, she will restructure her own involvement (reduce contact, change roles) rather than raise the grievance aloud, and will describe the change afterward as practical rather than as a response to hurt.

insights.headline: Money, dates, and durations are recorded with forensic exactness; her own feeling in the moment is either omitted or arrives late and startled.
insights.explanation: She gives exact figures across every experience — "two thousand yen" (E1), "forty minutes" commute (E2), "two hundred and six households... eleven days" (E5) — but her interior states are either absent at the time (no reaction recorded to being passed over in E2 until she 'began to read... regulations') or arrive as a delayed, almost clinical surprise: "which surprised me" (E3, at the funeral), "I thought, here it comes, finally. And then it didn't" (E5). The numbers are always contemporaneous; the feelings are always retrospective or denied.

evidence.quote: Two hundred and six households. I did it in eleven days.
At her funeral I cried, which surprised me.

insights.would_predict: Mental and Emotional Health: in a stress-inventory or mood-tracking exercise, she will log dates, tasks, and durations accurately for a difficult week but leave the same-day emotional field blank or minimal, filling it in only in later reflection.

insights.headline: The people she loved most are rendered through a single physical object or mark, never through what they said to her.
insights.explanation: Her grandmother is 'machine oil and rice starch' and cool hands (E1); Fujita-sensei is reduced to 'a mark' on her wrist from an old burn that she 'kept looking at' (E4); her husband becomes, in the space of one paragraph, a chair sent to the recycling shop and a thermos that falls out of a cupboard (E5). In none of these three most significant relationships does she quote a substantive thing the person said to her about her interior life — the intimacy is displaced onto objects and traces.

evidence.quote: she had burned her wrist once on a steam tray, years before, there was a mark, and I kept looking at the mark
the thermos he used for fishing fell out and hit the floor and I sat down on the kitchen floor

insights.would_predict: Faith and Spirituality or Family: asked to describe what her grandmother, Fujita-sensei, or Hiroshi believed or wanted for their own life, she will struggle to answer in their words and default back to a physical detail or task.

insights.headline: What looked in E1–E4 like a private taste for ledger-keeping is, by E5, a fully substituted grief process — the account book has replaced mourning as her instrument for love.
insights.explanation: E1 alone reads as a childhood quirk ('temperament'); E2–E4 alone read as professional competence and quiet resistance to being sidelined. Only E5 — where she processes her husband's death entirely through a spreadsheet of condolence money, a hakajimai executed like a work project, and an explicit admission she has not cried in four years — allows the claim that the ledger is not a coping strategy alongside grief but a substitute for it, because the corpus never shows the grief itself occurring, only its infrastructure.

evidence.quote: I have never in my life been comfortable with an open line.
It was work with a clear edge to it and I was extremely good at it.

insights.would_predict: Rest and Recreation: on the anniversary of Hiroshi's death, she will generate or complete an organizational task (updating the columbarium records, the neighborhood accounts) rather than take unstructured time, and will describe the day afterward primarily through what got done.

insights.headline: No experience contains a moment where someone helps her, though five decades of caretaking, illness, and administrative overload gave ample room for one to appear.
insights.explanation: She nurses her mother-in-law 'at the end' (E3), does eleven days of funeral logistics alone (E5), visits an abusive household four times until admitted (E4), and walks two hours alone as a child (E1) — every hard task in the corpus is solo. The one offer of help she reports, her sister-in-law's "you should rest" (E5, L10), is explicitly declined on-page. No experience shows her accepting aid, delegating under strain, or being cared for by another adult.

evidence.quote: My sister-in-law said, Sumie-san, you should rest, and I said thank you, and I did not rest, because — well, because the work was there.

insights.would_predict: Physical Health: if she becomes seriously ill or injured, she will attempt to manage her own paperwork, appointments, and household logistics rather than hand them to the brother-in-law, Ueda-san, or another available person, at least in the first weeks.

insights.headline: She names her own body only through what happens to other people's — her father's crushed hand, Fujita's burn scar, Hiroshi's knee — and never describes her own physical state across five decades.
insights.explanation: The corpus tracks other bodies with precision (father's 'two fingers,' 'autumn of nineteen sixty-three,' E1; the burn mark, E4; the knee, E3) but her own body appears only functionally — walking two hours, sitting on a kitchen floor, swimming at seventy-one 'in a swimming cap' with a dash and no further comment (E5). There is no report anywhere of her own illness, pain, appetite, or aging beyond that single deflected clause.

evidence.quote: He crushed two fingers on his left hand in, I think it was the autumn of nineteen sixty-three

insights.would_predict: Physical Health: in a health check-in or journal exercise, she will describe a family member's or friend's physical symptoms in more concrete detail than her own, even when directly asked about her own condition first.

insights.headline: Her signature genius is building the invisible structure that makes chaos survivable for others — and she consistently rates this work above the visible, credited alternative.
insights.explanation: The persimmon-colored notebook as a child (E1), the timetable 'over three nights... with a thermos' that she loved 'more than at my wedding' (E4), and the widowhood spreadsheet of 206 households (E5) are the same act at three life stages: converting overwhelming, relational chaos into a legible system. In each, this structural work is explicitly rated as more satisfying than the socially visible alternative available to her (marriage, principal's chair, public grief).

evidence.quote: the work I loved most in thirty-eight years was the timetable

insights.would_predict: Work and Career: offered a new volunteer or paid project, she will gravitate toward the role involving scheduling, records, or resource allocation over any role involving public representation, even if the latter pays or credits more.

facts.what_happened: The meeting was a miai, an arranged introduction.
The meeting took place in 1981 in a hotel in Umeda, with a photograph album present; his mother did most of the talking.
His name was Hiroshi.
Hiroshi was an engineer with the municipal waterworks bureau and, when it was his turn to speak, described the filtration system at the Kunijima plant at length.
The go-between made faces at Hiroshi to stop him talking.
The speaker states the marriage was restful.
The marriage was restful for forty years.
They married the following spring (1982).

Hiroshi's mother moved in with them in 1989 after his father died and lived with them eleven years; the speaker nursed her at the end; an understanding was reached around year six dividing responsibility for the kitchen and outside the door.
The speaker cried at the mother's funeral, which surprised her.
The speaker states "It didn't" regarding children.
The speaker states "We didn't" regarding children.
In the early years there was an expectation of children; the mother-in-law referenced the Nakamuras' grandchild indirectly; the speaker responded "oh, is that so, how nice."
At ages thirty-five and forty the question of children stopped being asked; the speaker noticed nobody had asked in a year, on a Tuesday, and bought a melon on the way home.
Hiroshi fished.

From around 1990 onward, every Sunday he went to Wakayama or the Yodo River with two men from the bureau, returned at four in the afternoon smelling of the sun, and cleaned the rods on newspaper in the genkan.
On Sundays the speaker graded work, read, went to the department store and looked at things without buying, and sat in the house with all the windows open and no one in it.
The speaker has never told anyone that Sunday was her favorite day, and that it was her favorite day because he was not there.
They spoke about the rain, his knee, and whether the hedge wanted cutting.
In forty years he did not ask her a question about her work that was not about the commute.
She did not ask him about the bureau.
In 1994, Hiroshi was passed over for section chief; the speaker learned about it from his colleague's wife at a New Year gathering, two months after.
The speaker said nothing to him about it.
She made a better dinner that week.
Her friend Fujita-sensei, a home economics teacher, used to ask her, "does your husband know you at all."
The speaker's response was "he knows the hedge wants cutting."
Fujita-sensei would laugh.
Around 2005, a colleague, Ōtsuka-sensei, told her, "sensei, you have given up so much."
The speaker became quite angry, which she says is not like her.
The speaker replied, "thank you for your concern."

insights.headline: She converts every major grief or injustice into an administrative task performed alone before witnesses are told.
insights.explanation: The child who walks two hours to repay a debt in secret (E1), the woman who files a transfer without mentioning it (E2), and the widow who arranges hakajimai — temple, stonemason, permits — before phoning her brother-in-law (E5) all show the same shape: private execution, then announcement. This is not simply thoroughness; in each case the concealment itself is chosen, not incidental, since she had opportunity to include others and declined.
insights.narrator_frame: In E5 she calls her brother-in-law's objection almost a joke: "I am consulting you now... which was not true" (L35-36); elsewhere she frames the secrecy as temperament or convenience, never naming it as a pattern.

evidence.quote: I told no one. For about a month.
I arranged the whole of it before I told anybody.

insights.falsifier: An instance where she brings in a collaborator or asks permission before acting on a significant decision affecting others, at the planning stage rather than after.
insights.would_predict: Health and Wellness: if she receives a serious personal diagnosis, she will research and decide on a course of treatment alone and present it to family as settled, rather than deliberating with them.

insights.headline: She treats being needed as more valuable than being credited, and repeatedly chooses the former over the latter when both are on offer.
insights.explanation: She volunteers for the 'difficult' school where 'you were not handed things, you were simply needed' (E2), calls the vice-principalship — invisible, no face — the truest description of herself (E4), and takes chairmanship offers from the neighborhood association only to hand the visible title to Ueda-san while doing the actual work herself (E5). In all three she has a path to visible authority (principal's exam, committee chair) and exchanges it for functional indispensability instead.
insights.narrator_frame: She says of the principal's exam: "I am not a face, I am a pair of hands" (E4, L29), and admits she has "never once corrected the impression" that this is about weakness rather than choice.

evidence.quote: you were not, ah, you were not handed things, you were simply needed
Ueda-san is chair. He is a good man and he cannot operate a spreadsheet and he telephones me on Sunday evenings.

insights.falsifier: An instance where she actively campaigns for a title or public credit rather than declining it while retaining the operational work.
insights.would_predict: Work and Career: in any future volunteer or advisory role, she will decline the named leadership position while becoming the person the actual title-holder depends on within weeks.

insights.headline: She describes herself as someone who does not object, while her life is a record of engineered, undeclared exits from the arrangements she claims to accept.
insights.explanation: She states plainly "I did not object" to twelve years of pouring tea (E2, L12-13) and frames her marriage as something she simply fit inside (E3). Yet the same person spent months reading obscure transfer regulations to escape the tea-pouring hierarchy (E2), used Sundays alone as a secretly cherished non-marital space (E3, L28), and later closed a family grave and dissolved a forty-year household's rituals unilaterally (E5) — none of which is 'not objecting,' all of which are self-authored departures dressed as continuity.
insights.narrator_frame: "I did not object" and later "He would have said the same about the river" (E3) — she frames both marriage and workplace hierarchy as mutual or accepted arrangements, not something she is working around.

evidence.quote: I have read things since where women say they objected and perhaps they did, but I did not.

insights.falsifier: A case where she names dissatisfaction directly to the person responsible, rather than resolving it through private, structural rerouting.
insights.would_predict: Relationships: in a current friendship or community conflict, she will restructure her own involvement (reduce contact, change roles) rather than raise the grievance aloud, and will describe the change afterward as practical rather than as a response to hurt.

insights.headline: Money, dates, and durations are recorded with forensic exactness; her own feeling in the moment is either omitted or arrives late and startled.
insights.explanation: She gives exact figures across every experience — "two thousand yen" (E1), "forty minutes" commute (E2), "two hundred and six households... eleven days" (E5) — but her interior states are either absent at the time (no reaction recorded to being passed over in E2 until she 'began to read... regulations') or arrive as a delayed, almost clinical surprise: "which surprised me" (E3, at the funeral), "I thought, here it comes, finally. And then it didn't" (E5). The numbers are always contemporaneous; the feelings are always retrospective or denied.
insights.narrator_frame: None — she never remarks on this asymmetry, and at one point flags her own flat affect as odd only in passing: "Is that a shocking thing" (E5, L13).

evidence.quote: Two hundred and six households. I did it in eleven days.

insights.falsifier: A passage where she reports an emotion in real time, with the same immediacy and specificity as a figure, rather than after the fact or as a negation.
insights.would_predict: Mental and Emotional Health: in a stress-inventory or mood-tracking exercise, she will log dates, tasks, and durations accurately for a difficult week but leave the same-day emotional field blank or minimal, filling it in only in later reflection.

insights.headline: The people she loved most are rendered through a single physical object or mark, never through what they said to her.
insights.explanation: Her grandmother is 'machine oil and rice starch' and cool hands (E1); Fujita-sensei is reduced to 'a mark' on her wrist from an old burn that she 'kept looking at' (E4); her husband becomes, in the space of one paragraph, a chair sent to the recycling shop and a thermos that falls out of a cupboard (E5). In none of these three most significant relationships does she quote a substantive thing the person said to her about her interior life — the intimacy is displaced onto objects and traces.
insights.narrator_frame: She notes the strangeness herself only once: "I can still smell them, is that a strange thing to say" (E1) — but does not connect it to the same displacement recurring with Fujita-sensei or her husband.

evidence.quote: she had burned her wrist once on a steam tray, years before, there was a mark, and I kept looking at the mark

insights.headline: What looked in E1–E4 like a private taste for ledger-keeping is, by E5, a fully substituted grief process — the account book has replaced mourning as her instrument for love.
insights.explanation: E1 alone reads as a childhood quirk ('temperament'); E2–E4 alone read as professional competence and quiet resistance to being sidelined. Only E5 — where she processes her husband's death entirely through a spreadsheet of condolence money, a hakajimai executed like a work project, and an explicit admission she has not cried in four years — allows the claim that the ledger is not a coping strategy alongside grief but a substitute for it, because the corpus never shows the grief itself occurring, only its infrastructure.
insights.narrator_frame: She names the substitution almost but not quite: "I don't think I have cried about Hiroshi. I've waited. Four years" (E5, L15-17), immediately followed by returning to task language: "I got up and made the tea."

evidence.quote: I have never in my life been comfortable with an open line.

insights.falsifier: A future account of unstructured, task-free grief for Hiroshi (or anyone) that does not resolve into a project, list, or arrangement.
insights.would_predict: Rest and Recreation: on the anniversary of Hiroshi's death, she will generate or complete an organizational task (updating the columbarium records, the neighborhood accounts) rather than take unstructured time, and will describe the day afterward primarily through what got done.

insights.headline: No experience contains a moment where someone helps her, though five decades of caretaking, illness, and administrative overload gave ample room for one to appear.
insights.explanation: She nurses her mother-in-law 'at the end' (E3), does eleven days of funeral logistics alone (E5), visits an abusive household four times until admitted (E4), and walks two hours alone as a child (E1) — every hard task in the corpus is solo. The one offer of help she reports, her sister-in-law's "you should rest" (E5, L10), is explicitly declined on-page. No experience shows her accepting aid, delegating under strain, or being cared for by another adult.
insights.narrator_frame: "My sister-in-law said, Sumie-san, you should rest, and I said thank you, and I did not rest" — offered as a small aside, not flagged as a pattern.

insights.would_predict: Physical Health: if she becomes seriously ill or injured, she will attempt to manage her own paperwork, appointments, and household logistics rather than hand them to the brother-in-law, Ueda-san, or another available person, at least in the first weeks.

insights.headline: She names her own body only through what happens to other people's — her father's crushed hand, Fujita's burn scar, Hiroshi's knee — and never describes her own physical state across five decades.
insights.explanation: The corpus tracks other bodies with precision (father's 'two fingers,' 'autumn of nineteen sixty-three,' E1; the burn mark, E4; the knee, E3) but her own body appears only functionally — walking two hours, sitting on a kitchen floor, swimming at seventy-one 'in a swimming cap' with a dash and no further comment (E5). There is no report anywhere of her own illness, pain, appetite, or aging beyond that single deflected clause.
insights.narrator_frame: "I've started swimming on Thursdays at the ward pool, which at seventy-one, in a swimming cap, is — well." — trails off rather than completes the thought about her own body.

evidence.quote: He crushed two fingers on his left hand in, I think it was the autumn of nineteen sixty-three
I've started swimming on Thursdays at the ward pool, which at seventy-one, in a swimming cap, is — well.

insights.falsifier: Any passage where she completes a sentence about her own physical sensation, limitation, or appearance with the same specificity given to others' bodies.
insights.would_predict: Physical Health: in a health check-in or journal exercise, she will describe a family member's or friend's physical symptoms in more concrete detail than her own, even when directly asked about her own condition first.

insights.headline: Her signature genius is building the invisible structure that makes chaos survivable for others — and she consistently rates this work above the visible, credited alternative.
insights.explanation: The persimmon-colored notebook as a child (E1), the timetable 'over three nights... with a thermos' that she loved 'more than at my wedding' (E4), and the widowhood spreadsheet of 206 households (E5) are the same act at three life stages: converting overwhelming, relational chaos into a legible system. In each, this structural work is explicitly rated as more satisfying than the socially visible alternative available to her (marriage, principal's chair, public grief).
insights.narrator_frame: "I would do it over three nights in February with the windows dark and a thermos, and when the last block went in I felt — I have never felt anything like it. Not at my wedding."

evidence.quote: the work I loved most in thirty-eight years was the timetable
It was work with a clear edge to it and I was extremely good at it.

insights.falsifier: An account of comparable satisfaction or flow from a purely relational or public-facing achievement, unconnected to systems or record-keeping.
insights.would_predict: Work and Career: offered a new volunteer or paid project, she will gravitate toward the role involving scheduling, records, or resource allocation over any role involving public representation, even if the latter pays or credits more.

patterns.title: You turn grief and injustice into paperwork, then present it as finished.
patterns.description: At eight or nine you walked two hours alone to repay a debt in secret and told no one for a month. Fifty years later you closed your husband's family grave — temple, stonemason, permits — before phoning his brother, then told him, "I am consulting you now," by your own account "which was not true." Same shape both times: act alone, announce after. Your brother-in-law's objection — "you might have consulted" — was the one moment someone named this to your face, and you deflected it with a joke rather than answering it.
patterns.watch_for: a future case where you loop someone in at the planning stage, not after — that would complicate this.
patterns.prediction: if you get a serious diagnosis, you'll research and decide on treatment alone and present it as settled.

patterns.title: You keep trading visible credit for indispensability, and calling it a preference.
patterns.description: You volunteered for the school "where you were not handed things, you were simply needed" instead of taking the third-year homeroom you'd already built the folder for. You turned down the principal's exam twice with excuses you later admit weren't fully honest ("that was a lie, obviously"), saying "I am not a face, I am a pair of hands." You let Ueda-san chair the neighborhood association while you write the rules, run the accounts, and take his Sunday calls. Each time there was a path to the title and you chose the function instead.
patterns.watch_for: you campaigning for a title rather than declining it while keeping the work.
patterns.prediction: in any new volunteer role, you'll decline the named position but become the person the title-holder depends on within weeks.

patterns.title: You say you don't object, while your life is a record of quiet, engineered exits.
patterns.description: "I did not object" to twelve years of pouring tea — and then spent months studying transfer regulations to leave that hierarchy without a conversation. You call your marriage something you simply fit inside — and Sunday, the one day alone, was "my favorite day and it was my favorite day because he was not there," something you say you've never told anyone. Not objecting and rerouting your entire life around a friction point are not the same thing, even though you narrate them as the same choice.
patterns.watch_for: a case where you name the grievance directly to the person responsible instead of restructuring around it.
patterns.prediction: in a current friendship or community conflict, you'll quietly reduce your own involvement rather than raise the issue aloud, then call it practical afterward.

patterns.title: You log numbers with total precision and your own feelings almost never, or late.
patterns.description: "Two thousand yen." "Forty minutes." "Two hundred and six households... eleven days." Meanwhile the thermos falling out of the cupboard gets you onto the kitchen floor for twenty minutes, and then: "I thought, here it comes, finally. And then it didn't." Four years, no crying, by your own count. The figures arrive in real time; the feeling, when it arrives at all, arrives afterward and surprises you — "At her funeral I cried, which surprised me."
patterns.watch_for: a passage where you report an emotion as it happens, with the same immediacy as a figure.
patterns.prediction: in any mood-tracking or check-in exercise, you'll log tasks and times accurately and leave the same-day feeling blank.

patterns.title: The people you loved most come through as objects, not words they said to you.
patterns.description: Your grandmother is "machine oil and rice starch" and cool hands. Fujita-sensei becomes a burn mark on her wrist that you "kept looking at." Your husband becomes a chair sent to the recycling shop and a thermos on the floor. In none of these three relationships do you quote something substantial they said to you about their inner life.
patterns.watch_for: a memory centered on an actual remembered conversation rather than a physical trace.
patterns.prediction: asked what your grandmother, Fujita-sensei, or Hiroshi wanted for their own life, you'll default back to a sensory detail rather than their words.

patterns.title: The ledger has replaced mourning, not accompanied it.
patterns.description: Early on, keeping accounts reads as temperament — a notebook, a taste for order. By widowhood it's the whole apparatus: a spreadsheet for condolence money, a grave closure run like a project, and the flat statement "I don't think I have cried about Hiroshi. I've waited. Four years" — followed immediately by "I got up and made the tea." Nowhere in five accounts does unstructured grief actually happen; only its infrastructure does.
patterns.watch_for: an account of grief for Hiroshi, or anyone, that doesn't resolve into a task.
patterns.prediction: on the anniversary of his death, you'll complete an organizational task rather than take unstructured time, and describe the day afterward through what got done.

patterns.title: No one has helped you, in fifty years, in any of the hard stretches.
patterns.description: You nursed your mother-in-law alone. You did eleven days of funeral logistics alone. You went to a student's apartment four evenings running, alone, until someone opened the door. The one offer of help on record — your sister-in-law's "you should rest" — you declined on the spot: "I did not rest, because — well, because the work was there."
patterns.watch_for: any account of accepting help mid-crisis, letting someone else take a task.
patterns.prediction: if you become seriously ill, you'll try to manage your own appointments and paperwork rather than hand them off, at least at first.

patterns.title: You describe other people's bodies precisely and your own almost never.
patterns.description: Your father's "two fingers," "autumn of nineteen sixty-three." Fujita's burn mark. Your own body appears only in what it does — walking two hours, sitting on a kitchen floor — until one line about swimming at seventy-one "in a swimming cap" trails off: "which... is — well."
patterns.watch_for: a completed sentence about your own physical sensation or limitation with the same detail given to others.
patterns.prediction: in a health check-in, you'll describe someone else's symptoms in more detail than your own, even when asked about yourself first.

patterns.title: Your clearest genius is building invisible structure that makes chaos survivable for other people — and you rate it above the visible alternative every time.
patterns.description: The persimmon notebook as a child. The class timetable you built over three nights with a thermos, feeling something you say you never felt "at my wedding." The 206-household spreadsheet after Hiroshi died. Each time, structural work beat the socially visible option you also had available — marriage, the principal's chair, public grief.
patterns.watch_for: comparable satisfaction from something purely relational or public-facing, unconnected to systems.
patterns.prediction: offered a new project, you'll gravitate to the scheduling or records role over the public-facing one, even if the latter pays or credits more.
